<reason>CON won by tying the debate tightly to the motion as written and to the three-year horizon. Its 2021–22 evidence (8–9% inflation, spiral never arrived, expectations held, unemployment barely moved) directly undercut PRO's 1970s-based spiral story, and CON's pressure question on defining "modest" forced PRO into a position ("stop blind tightening if expectations are anchored, yes") that CON credibly reframed as the flexible mandate CON was defending, leaving the motion's "even if" clause reduced to refusing to ease at 3% inflation with unemployment up a full point — which CON linked to the ECB 2011 failure mode. PRO was disciplined, answered A1/A2 cleanly, and had a coherent "when you act" closing (expectations move before surveys show it), and its broad-checks-vs-targeted-benefits distinction was a fair answer to the alleged contradiction. But PRO's core mechanism remained largely assertive against CON's recent-history counterexample, and PRO never fully rebutted the point that credibility was maintained by a reaction function that eased as labor cooled. CON's late clipping was minor. Overall CON made the decision easier and carried the weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.4/B5.2: CON took PRO's own answer in [A4.1] ("stop blind tightening if expectations are anchored") and showed that PRO's residual commitment — holding restrictive rates with unemployment up a point and inflation near 3% while expectations stay anchored — is exactly the ECB-2011 scenario, converting PRO's hierarchy into either CON's flexible mandate or a recession recipe.</best_rebuttal>
